title: Universal invites you to experience 'Big Brother: The Ride'
summary:
By Robert Niles: How would you feel about a theme park ride that changes based on what the park knows about you?

Universal has a plan for that. In "Ride Vehicle Artificial Intelligence Entity Systems and Methods," Universal details its latest proposal for creating a ride that uses AI and a guest tracking system to create unique experiences for riders.

Universal's proposed ride system could track guests' presence on a ride via cameras or wearable RFID devices. Networked to other guest monitoring systems in the park, the ride could learn which lands of rides a specific guest prefers and the people with which a guest is visiting the park that day. Merge all that with whatever other preference data the park has on a guest, and the ride has plenty of details that it could use to tailor a unique experience.

It's the dark ride equivalent of a "Choose Your Adventure" book, except it's the book that's doing the choosing, based on all the intel that the publisher has collected about you as an individual consumer.


Image from Universal's patent application

The patent application mentions the example of a guest who fears clowns. In an evil embodiment, Universal's system could generate an AI clown on screen in the ride vehicle to harass that guest. In a kinder scenario, the ride could substitute an alternate character in a scene in lieu of clowns.

Customizations could be for groups as well as individuals, based on shared interests or preferences of the people on the ride. The system could manage lighting, sound, animation and projection systems within a ride vehicle and in the surrounding show scenery to deliver its custom experiences. The ride also could alert other park systems, too. If the ride went down or even was stopped too long, it could alert the park's customer service team that its riders did not get the experience that the park wanted to provide, so that some alternate experience or compensation might be offered.

The system also includes the option of a guest choosing what information to share with the park and to limit how it might be used. For example, a parent could opt to have a ride character greet them by name but not mention out loud the names of their children in a shared ride vehicle.

After the ride, uptime and customer satisfaction data could help train the ride's AI to create a better and more reliable and engaging experience for future riders.

You can read all the details of the many ways that Universal plans to use the data it collects to customize guest experiences in the patent application: Ride Vehicle Artificial Intelligence Entity Systems and Methods.

title: Revenue falls at Universal's theme parks
summary:
By Robert Niles: Revenue and earnings fell at Universal's theme parks in the back half of this summer when compared with the same period one year ago.

Universal Studios owner Comcast reported this morning that revenue from its theme parks segment dropped 4.4% for the three months ending September 30, to $2.597 billion. With a 2.3% increase in operating expenses, Adjusted EBITDA dropped 17.1% for the quarter, to $780 million.

"While we continue to see near-term demand pressure across portions of the parks business, including in Orlando and certain international markets, we view these trends as temporary rather than structural, due to the confluence of a few factors," Comcast CEO Michael J. Cavanagh said. "In addition to the macroeconomic and geopolitical headwinds we have referenced in the past, we believe two other factors have contributed to this recent softness.

"First, we believe competitors were quicker to anticipate and recognize softness and demand, and adapt their marketing strategies. And second, we continue to work through capacity challenges and ride throughput at Epic, given the complexities of opening the most technologically advanced theme park ever built. We are taking action to address both of these challenges."

One year ago, the third quarter was the first full quarter for the new Epic Universe theme park at Universal Orlando, which boosted revenue for that quarter.

"Attendance, guest spending, and overall financial performance remain materially above where they were two years ago, and guest satisfaction continues to rise," Cavanagh said. "Looking ahead, we expect performance to strengthen as we move through 2027, with a return to growth in the second half of the year."

title: There's a new way to insure a roller coaster park
summary:
By Robert Niles: If you've ever struggled trying to buy car or home insurance, imagine trying to buy insurance for a theme park.

But every business needs insurance, including theme and amusement parks. Yet calling your average business insurance company to write a policy for your roller coasters and dark rides is more likely to elicit a "you've got to be kidding me" than a "what day would you like your policy to start?"

Apparently many parks, from small family entertainment centers to large resorts, have been struggling to get fair and affordable policies for their operations. So the industry's leading trade organization now is getting into the attraction insurance industry.

IAAPA - the industry organization behind the annual IAAPA Expos - has announced a new business, IAAPA Insurance Solutions. Launching this year for North American properties, IAAPA Insurance Solutions is a licensed insurance agency established through a joint venture between IAAPA and Higginbotham Insurance Agency. The official kickoff will be at the IAAPA Expo 2026 in November in Orlando.

"IAAPA members have told us for years that the insurance marketplace doesn�t always reflect the realities of operating an attraction," IAAPA Chief Financial Officer Josh Powers said. "IAAPA Insurance Solutions gives us an opportunity to address that challenge with a long-term industry focused approach rather than a short-term solution. Most importantly, the value it created through this program comes back to support our members and the industry we serve."

IAAPA Insurance Solutions will offer policies to IAAPA members operating amusement and theme parks, water parks, family entertainment centers, zoos and aquariums, museums and science centers, nature and adventure attractions, as well as to manufacturers, suppliers and consultants in the attractions industry. Interested IAAPA members can learn more at iaapainsurance.com.

title: Can anything save Six Flags now?
summary:
By Robert Niles: Okay, this is not exactly news, but let's say it anyway. Six Flags is in trouble.

The company's stock price closed trading today at $7.86 a share. That's down more than 70% from its high in the past 12 months. That's also down 86% from the $57.63 the stock traded at after the Cedar Fair/Six Flags merger closed in July 2024.

When a company loses nearly 90% of its value, that is very, very bad news for the company. Activist investors demanded a sale earlier this year, but that strategy works only if someone else on Wall Street sees potential value in a company. Right now, it seems that no one is buying into Six Flags.

Despite the gruesome stock performance, Six Flags' individual theme parks are profitable. The company is making money where it counts - with guests coming into the gates and spending money inside the parks. So what's the problem?

Two things. First, as we have mentioned many times before, debt. Interest payments on the nearly $5 billion that the company owes is wiping out the parks' quarterly profits. Add to that the company's new, second big problem, which is anticipated legal liabilities. Investors are scared of what the company might end up having to pay in legal judgments over its now-closed X2 roller coaster as well as the fatal incident on Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath coaster last week.

The company was trading in the $15-16 range before the X2 news blew up last month. That's not great, but it is double where the stock price is now.

To be fair, Six Flags' nearest competitor, United Parks & Resorts, ain't exactly doing great, either. United's stock closed today at $31.76, down 40% for the year. Given that the Dow is up more than 12% for the past 12 months, that's awful performance. United's main selling point these days, as an investment, seems to be, "Hey, at least we're not Six Flags?"

The theme park industry took on an enormous amount of debt to get through the pandemic. While the Disney and Universal parks are part of larger corporations with outside income and financing leverage, Six Flags and United have to rely on theme park income to pay their way out of their debt. While their parks are profitable, they are not printing the volume of cash that the companies need to erase their debt and move forward.

That said, United's stock price is trading around its pre-pandemic level. But Six Flags is trading at about one-seventh of what its predecessor Cedar Fair traded for before the lockdowns. (Six Flags now trades under the same FUN symbol used by Cedar Fair, which tells you everything about who really bought whom in that merger.)

It's hard for me to see much of a future for the Six Flags company at this point. But with profitable theme parks, many sitting on ridiculously valuable real estate, Six Flags very well be a company where the parts are more valuable than the whole. Especially if the parts can be sold off without carrying any responsibility for the company's debt and liability burdens.

So if you are a wealthy individual or business in a community where Six Flags owns a park, now's the time to call.

As a theme park fan, I would much prefer that Six Flags sells a park to someone who wants to keep running it rather than selling to a developer who just wants the real estate. If Six Flags can start making those sales now, then it might have the choice. But if Six Flags waits until its debt and legal burdens force it into bankruptcy court, that might no longer be an option. At that point, high bids win, even if theme park fans lose.

The combination of Cedar Fair and the old Six Flags failed to produce any economies of scale to justify that merger. If anything, the deal simply has exposed the former Cedar Fair parks to liabilities from legacy Six Flags parks. As a theme park fan, I would love to see this deal unwound, as quickly as possible. Let's get great parks such as Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm, Canada's Wonderland, Six Flags Fiesta Texas, and Kings Island into the hands of private owners with the resources to invest and maintain these parks. And let's do it before the whole lot ends in bankruptcy court, where fans might end up losing some of the parks that they love.

Because the way that Six Flags is headed right now, it's hard to see any other way that this story ends.

title: Disney inks deal with Shutterfly as new PhotoPass partner
summary:
By Robert Niles: If you want to use that family photo in front of Cinderella Castle for your Christmas card this year, Disney has just saved you a step.

Disney and Shutterfly today announced a deal that makes Shutterfly the official photo gift partner of Walt Disney World and Disneyland. The deal will extend to the Disney Cruise Line and Aulani next year.

Under the deal, Disney parks guests who use Disney's PhotoPass service will be able to transfer their PhotoPass photos automatically to their Shutterfly account. That service is live today at Disneyland and Walt Disney World, and will start in early 2027 for DCL and Aulani.

In addition, Shutterfly is adding a bunch of new Disney-themed photo gift products, including ones themed to the Disney theme parks. Popular products include those holiday cards, photo books, and calendars. Users can find those new Disney-themed designs via a new Disney shopping hub on Shutterfly.com.

title: How to stay safe on a roller coaster
summary:
By Robert Niles: Given the recent news, I thought it was time to update our regular safety advice for theme park visitors.

Worried about your safety on a roller coaster? The numbers say that you will be safer on the ride than on the road heading to the park. But if statistics are not enough to reassure you, here are my tips for concerned roller coaster riders.

1. Read the safety sign

Every roller coaster and thrill ride will have a sign at the ride's queue entrance that lists the warnings and restrictions for riding. Read this sign. If there is anything that applies to you and tells you not to ride, then step away. Don't get in line. Find something else to do in the park. But if nothing on the warning sign applies to you, proceed to step 2.

2. Try the test seat

Most major coasters will have a test seat located somewhere near the ride's entrance. At the best park, these are located out of view of the people in line, so you can try the seat in privacy. So you might need to ask a park employee near the queue entrance where to find it. The test seat allows you to see how you will fit on the side and in the seat's restraint system. If you feel really uncomfortable here, it's not going to be any better on the ride, so - again - step away and pick something else to do. But if it feels good, go get in the line.

3. Don't get into a fight in the queue

This may seem obvious, but having worked in theme parks and visited them for years, I have seen way more people get hurt in fights than on rides. Whether it is line jumpers or people not minding their personal space, queues can provoke a lot of conflict. Be the better person and do not escalate a bad situation. Report bad behavior to park employees, but do not make policing the queue your job.

4. Follow employees' instructions

I know that it can be tough to hear bad station loudspeakers, but do you best to do what park employees tell you while waiting. At the load platform, it will be easier to hear the employees who will speak to you directly. Listen to their instructions and do what they say. If you cannot, or have any type of problem, please - politely - let an employee know. At some point in the queue, you might be asked to stash all personal belongings in a cubby or locker. Again, follow the instructions. No one on the ride wants to get hit by your phone when it flies out of your hand.

5. Don't try to cheat the restraint

A park employee should check to ensure that your restraint is fastened correctly. Don't try to cheat this process to get "extra space" for more airtime on the ride. If a restraint is so uncomfortable that you are worried about your safety on the ride, please let the employees know so that they can let you out and you can skip the ride.

6. Relax

Once you are safely seated and secured, your own stress is your worst enemy on a coaster. Tensing your body can cause you to strain muscles and leave you in pain after the ride. Try to relax your joints while riding. If you wish, hold on to the grab bar if that makes you feel more secure.

When the ride is done, listen to and follow the instructions when you exit the coaster train. Get your stuff out of the locker or cubby and head to your next adventure in the park!

Do take a moment to check how you feel first, though. If you need to sit and take a moment, do it. For many theme park fans, it's not one coaster ride that leaves them feeling sick. It's trying to do too many things too quickly.

The better you take care of yourself before a thrill ride, the better you will be in handling it. Stay well hydrated and protected from the sun. Rest regularly - you'll be on your feet a lot during a theme park visit.

Stuff like dehydration, sunburns, heat exhaustion and blistered feet are - by far - the leading injuries in theme parks. Don't forget to do what you need to prevent those common injuries, too.

Again, ride data shows that injury rates are far higher on public roads than on roller coasters. But just like you should wear seat belts and follow traffic laws to help ensure your safety in the car, following the advice above can help ensure that you walk away safe, and smiling, from your next roller coaster ride.

* * *

title: Rope Drop: It's time to wine, dine, and dash at Disney
summary:
By Robert Niles: Before I preview the week ahead, I want to recap a few items from last week's theme park news.

First, congratulations to our friend Steve Tatham, is joining the faculty at the University of Southern California as the Director the Themed Entertainment Program in the USC School of Cinematic Arts' Interactive Media & Games Division.

Steve helped lead the creation of Universal Orlando's new Epic Universe theme park as its Executive Creative Director of Epic Universe, following a run as Vice President of Creative for Universal Studios Japan. Before joining Universal, Steve worked for Walt Disney Imagineering. At USC, he will oversee the school's BFA program in Themed Entertainment, which teaches students to develop immersive cinematic experiences at locations such as theme parks, zoos, retail, museums, and restaurants.

Here is my conversation with Steve at Epic Universe's opening.

Keeping with the L.A.-area theme park crew, former Walt Disney Imagineering president Bob Weis has started a podcast called Dream Chasing, after his recent book. His first guest is former Imagineer Kathy Mangum. I am working to schedule Bob for an upcoming episode of our Theme Park Insider Podcast, but in the meantime, please give him a listen over at his new home.

Looking ahead, it's time for another runDisney event at the Walt Disney World Resort. This time, it's the Wine & Dine Half Marathon Weekend, from October 22-25. If you are visiting, remember that runDisney events bring large crowds to the parks, especially in the mornings. Good luck to all the runners.

Back here in California, on Friday, the Indiana Jones Adventure reopens at Disneyland after a refurbishment.

Planning a trip?

Here are current and upcoming refurbishments at Disney and Universal parks in the U.S.:

Universal�s Horror Make-Up Show is closed at Universal Studios Florida. Estimated reopening in winter 2026.
Carousel of Progress is closed at Walt Disney World�s Magic Kingdom. New show debuts in 2027.

event_model_payload.summary:
By Robert Niles: Before I preview the week ahead, I want to recap a few items from last week's theme park news.

First, congratulations to our friend Steve Tatham, is joining the faculty at the University of Southern California as the Director the Themed Entertainment Program in the USC School of Cinematic Arts' Interactive Media & Games Division.

Steve helped lead the creation of Universal Orlando's new Epic Universe theme park as its Executive Creative Director of Epic Universe, following a run as Vice President of Creative for Universal Studios Japan. Before joining Universal, Steve worked for Walt Disney Imagineering. At USC, he will oversee the school's BFA program in Themed Entertainment, which teaches students to develop immersive cinematic experiences at locations such as theme parks, zoos, retail, museums, and restaurants.

Here is my conversation with Steve at Epic Universe's opening.

Keeping with the L.A.-area theme park crew, former Walt Disney Imagineering president Bob Weis has started a podcast called Dream Chasing, after his recent book. His first guest is former Imagineer Kathy Mangum. I am working to schedule Bob for an upcoming episode of our Theme Park Insider Podcast, but in the meantime, please give him a listen over at his new home.

Looking ahead, it's time for another runDisney event at the Walt Disney World Resort. This time, it's the Wine & Dine Half Marathon Weekend, from October 22-25. If you are visiting, remember that runDisney events bring large crowds to the parks, especially in the mornings. Good luck to all the runners.
